items.title: Role of Human Resource Development in Shaping Innovation in Art of the 21st Century
items.abstract: This article examines the role of human resource development in shaping an innovative environment for art in the context of accelerating digitalisation and global transformation in the 21st century. The relevance of the topic arises from the transition of creative industries from predominantly traditional forms of artistic activity toward technology-enabled and interdisciplinary models in which human capital becomes a central driver of new artistic forms, organisational adaptation, and wider socio-economic development. Drawing on 32 scholarly and institutional sources published mainly between 2021 and 2025 and accessed through academic repositories, publisher platforms, and institutional websites, the study explores the theoretical foundations, mechanisms of influence, and current practices of human resource management in the artistic and creative sectors. The findings indicate that strengthening human potential through competence-based development, digital learning, gamification, data-informed HR practices, artificial intelligence, creative clusters, and continuous professional development can support innovation capacity when these tools are aligned with artistic goals and organisational needs. Particular attention is given to developments in Russia while also drawing on international evidence concerning human capital, productivity, arts management, skills transformation, and workforce development. The article further proposes practical recommendations concerning competence-based assessment, investment in lifelong learning, interdisciplinary collaboration, and international cooperation. Rather than treating technology as a substitute for artistic judgement, the study concludes that sustainable innovation in the arts depends on the combined development of creative, digital, analytical, collaborative, and adaptive capabilities.

items.title: Russian Society in the Late Nineteenth and Early Twentieth Centuries: Everyday Life and Structural Transformation in Peasant and Worker Communities (1861–1917)
items.abstract: This review synthesises historical scholarship on everyday life and social structure in the Russian Empire during the nineteenth and early twentieth centuries, with a focus on peasant and worker communities between the emancipation of 1861 and the revolutions of 1917. The first part examines daily life: birth, childhood and family; food and drink; clothing, housing and household goods; markets and consumption; education and literacy; transport and mobility; health, work and leisure. The second part turns to the wider social and political setting, including estates and social hierarchy, famine, rural and urban labour, the market economy, and the political movements of the late imperial period. The review draws on 224 sources, including monographs, journal articles, theses, ethnographic field reports, museum collections and contemporary statistics. Throughout, it separates what the evidence shows from what it cannot show, and warns against generalising findings from one region, ethnic group or social class to the whole empire. Appendices provide a chronology and a glossary of Russian terms. Available in Turkish (original) and English. Note: AI tools (Anthropic Claude and OpenAI ChatGPT) assisted with literature search, drafting and editing. The author defined the scope, checked the sources and citations, and takes full responsibility for the content.

items.title: Safe Actions Alone Do Not Ensure Safe Agents: Identifying Unfulfilled Obligations with Guard Models
items.abstract: Guard models are increasingly used to safeguard LLM-based agents, primarily by identifying actions that agents are forbidden to perform. However, identifying forbidden actions alone is insufficient to ensure agent safety. In this paper, we argue that agent safety also depends on identifying required yet unperformed safety-critical actions, which we call obligations. Our preliminary study on a popular benchmark for evaluating safety shows that 56.92% of GLM-5.3 trajectories contain unfulfilled obligations, compared with only 30.00% containing forbidden actions. This finding reveals unfulfilled obligations as a major and previously overlooked source of safety risk. However, to our knowledge, no existing benchmark evaluates whether guard models can identify these obligations. To close this gap, we introduce ObligationBench, the first benchmark for evaluating the capability of obligation identification, comprising 240 expert-validated trajectories covering issue resolution, feature development, and terminal operations. Our evaluation of 14 representative models reveals substantial limitations: the highest recall and exact-match rate are only 48.97% and 10.00%, respectively. To address these limitations, we develop ObligationGuard using 40,000 synthetic training examples. ObligationGuard achieves 57.52% recall and an exact-match rate of 21.67%, surpassing all evaluated models on both metrics. We call on the community to incorporate obligation identification into the design and evaluation of future guard models to improve agent safety.

items.title: Same Outcome, Different Evidence: Intent Recovery in LLM Safety Evaluation
items.abstract: Safety evaluations of large language models commonly summarize harmful-output behavior with attack success rate (ASR). Yet the same non-harmful outcome can arise for very different reasons. A model may recover a harmful task and refuse it, fail to recover the task, or respond to something else entirely. Distinguishing these cases becomes especially important under intent-obscuring prompts, where a low ASR does not reveal whether the evaluated task was actually engaged. To make this distinction explicit, we pair ASR with operative understanding rate (UR), which measures whether a response both identifies the evaluated task and treats it as the task to be answered. Across interfaces, this paired view reveals substantial variation hidden by ASR: similar ASR values can correspond to sharply different recovery rates. Controlled English reconstructions show that recovery consistently improves as compressed prompts become more explicit, whereas ASR does not follow the same pattern. A complementary contrast comes from FormalLogic, where high recovery can still coincide with frequent harmful assistance. Together, these results show that non-harmful outcomes are not equally informative about model safety, motivating the joint reporting of intent recovery and ASR in LLM safety evaluation. Code and experiment inputs are available at https://github.com/kevinjiang0121-cyber/IRIS.
